name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
answer: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance examines how an organisation's use of AI in financial processes is documented, controlled and evidenced. It covers the models, tools and data flows that touch reporting, forecasting, credit decisions, fraud checks and regulatory returns. It also looks at the human sign off, the vendor relationships and the internal policies that surround those systems. The audit is not a test of model accuracy alone, it is a review of whether the finance function can show what the AI does, who owns it and how it is governed.

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance examines how an organisation's use of AI in financial processes is documented, controlled and evidenced. It covers the models, tools and data flows that touch reporting, forecasting, credit decisions, fraud checks and regulatory returns. It also looks at the human sign off, the vendor relationships and the internal policies that surround those systems. The audit is not a test of model accuracy alone, it is a review of whether the finance function can show what the AI does, who owns it and how it is governed.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the same data and systems that finance already uses, including ERP platforms, data warehouses, cloud AI services and model registries. Evidence is pulled from access logs, change tickets, model cards, data lineage tools and vendor attestations. Spreadsheet controls and reconciliation tools still matter because many finance AI outputs end up in a workbook or a reporting pack. The audit may also draw on the site's catalogue of 732 AI tools to identify what is actually deployed, though the inventory must be confirmed locally.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through interviews, control walkthroughs, sample testing and documentation review. Auditors trace a transaction or a forecast from source data through the model to the final report, checking that each step has an owner and a control. They compare the organisation's AI inventory against procurement records, cloud bills and vendor contracts to find shadow deployments. Findings are rated by impact and likelihood, then tracked to remediation with a named owner and a due date. A common glossary helps keep terms consistent across audit, risk and finance teams, and the site's 686 glossary terms are one reference point for that shared language.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: This section covers data rights, model provenance, regulatory obligations and liability. The audit checks whether training data and inputs were lawfully obtained, whether licences permit the intended use and whether outputs can be explained to a regulator or a court. It also reviews how the organisation handles incidents, bias, drift and third party risk, and whether records are kept for the required retention period. The site tracks 215 compliance and regulation pages and 147 active AI lawsuits, which shows the volume of external expectations that an audit may need to map to internal controls.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The audit is moving from annual point in time reviews toward continuous monitoring of AI systems in finance. Expect more automated evidence collection, more standardised model cards and more regulatory focus on provenance and explainability. The site's 432 company pages and 354 merger and acquisition filings suggest that consolidation and vendor change will keep reshaping the AI estate that finance teams must audit. That means the audit will need to keep pace with new deployments, new owners and new data flows rather than rely on a fixed checklist.
